common_name: Dorset Naga Pepper (UK-Bred Superhot Capsicum chinense)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense superhots germinate slowly and need consistent warmth.

directions: Give Dorset Naga a long, warm season indoors before transplanting, since it needs more heat units than a standard habanero to fully ripen its fruit to deep red. This English-developed selection was bred from Bangladeshi naga stock and yields smoother, more elongated pods than typical wrinkled bhut jolokia types, with fruity aroma alongside intense heat. Stake plants once fruit load builds, and pick some pods slightly early if frost threatens since later flushes often fail to color up in short seasons. It is best suited to collectors in long, hot-summer regions or to greenhouse culture where a longer ripening window can be guaranteed.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, as this Trinidad strain is slow to establish and needs a long warm season.

directions: 7 Pot Barrackpore takes its name from the Barrackpore district of Trinidad and is prized among superhot growers for pods that are less bumpy and wrinkled than most other 7 Pot strains, ripening from green to a glossy orange-red. Its heat arrives with a noticeably smoky, savory edge that Trinidad cooks favor for pepper sauces rather than fresh eating. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and stunted pod set on this variety. Because plants are tall and heavily branched once mature, stake or cage them early to keep the fruit-laden limbs from snapping in wind.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Chocolate Bhutlah Pepper (Ghost x Trinidad Scorpion Superhot Hybrid)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Bhutlah is among the slowest superhots to mature and needs the longest season possible.

directions: Bhutlah, sometimes sold as Chocolate Bhutlah, is a deliberate cross of bhut jolokia (ghost pepper) and Trinidad Scorpion lines, producing small, extremely gnarled dark-brown pods that rank among the most searing chiles grown by home superhot enthusiasts. Because the fruit is slow to size up and slower still to fully color from green to chocolate-brown, gardeners in short-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture so plants can be moved to protect them from early frost. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since chinense superhots are prone to root stress that shows up as blossom drop weeks later. Handle harvested pods with gloves, as oleoresin transfer from Bhutlah is unusually persistent even after washing.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since Moruga Scorpion strains germinate erratically without warmth.

directions: This is a yellow-fruited selection of the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion, sharing the same bumpy, tailed pod shape and ferocious heat as the original red strain but ripening to a bright golden-yellow instead. Growers often note the yellow form carries a slightly more citrusy, less smoky flavor than red Moruga types, making it popular for hot sauces where color as well as heat matters. Give plants the same long, warm growing season and rich soil that other Trinidad superhots require, and expect a later, more compact fruit set than milder chinense varieties. Because pod color can be the only visible way to distinguish it from other Moruga strains, keep seed-saved plants isolated from red-fruited relatives to preserve the true-to-type yellow trait.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60°F.

directions: Adjuma is a traditional pepper of Guadeloupe and Martinique, prized in Antillean kitchens for a strikingly fruity, floral aroma alongside solid habanero-level heat. Its squat, deeply wrinkled orange-yellow pods form in clusters and are typically used fresh, muddled into vinegar-based hot sauces rather than dried, so plan for repeated light harvests through the season instead of one large drying batch. Like other chinense types it thrives in consistent warmth and humidity, so mulch heavily and water deeply but infrequently to avoid the stress that triggers blossom drop. Choose Adjuma over a standard habanero when the goal is a more perfumed, less sharply citrusy aroma to complement Caribbean-style marinades and condiments.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
